To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) thrips prefer non-infested plants, and 2) JA-mediated defenses in the tomato host plant play an important role in mediating this preference.
the Western flower thrip, a key insect pest in tomato production, is repelled by its own induced defenses, and this repellence depends on the JA-mediated signaling pathway.
thrips infestation of tomato plants induces JA defenses that alter trichome densities and the production of tricho-malate volatiles.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the induction and consequences of plant-mediated intraspecies interactions between thrips, and the role of trichomes therein.
the induction of JA-mediated defenses and the consequences for subsequent feeding herbivore performance, and how this can affect plant-herbivore interactions.
how herbivores can shape the evolution of plant defenses, and how plant defenses can affect the behavior and fitness of conspecifics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
thrips infestation induces JA-mediated defenses in wild-type plants which, in turn, increase trichome densities and the production of triterpenes.

the induction of JA-associated plant defense responses in tomato by thrips infestation alters the host plant suitability and feeding preferences of their conspecific, and this is mediated by the production of tricho-dermally associated volatiles.
thrips infestation induces JA-associated defenses in the host plant, which in turn affect subsequent conspecifics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the JA pathway plays a major role in the defense of tomato against Western flower thrips, and this pathway is also involved in the intraspecific interactions among thrips.
herbivore-induced plant defenses can determine the performance of subsequent herbivores.
thrips can affect their performance on plants through a complex interaction with the plant defense signaling network.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the JA pathway can mediate plant responses to insect herbivory and that these responses can have consequences for the performance of subsequent feeding insects, thus affecting the dynamics of plant-insect interactions.
JA defenses can be induced by a herbivore and that these defenses can affect the foraging behavior of its conspecifics.

JA-mediated plant defense responses can alter host plant suitability and insect behavior in a complex way, with implications for insect population dynamics and the evolution of insect-plant interactions.
